title: Minimum 2-Year Analysis of S2-Alar-Iliac Screw Fixation for Adult Spinal Deformity
condition_or_topic: S2AI screw fixation for pelvic stabilization in adult spinal deformity surgery
clinical_background: Long spinal fusions for adult spinal deformity can develop pseudarthrosis at the lumbosacral junction, making pelvic fixation important for distal stability. Traditional iliac screws can be difficult to connect to the proximal construct and may be prominent; prior reports describe clinically significant prominence in up to 20% of cases. S2AI screws begin deeper and more medially, potentially reducing prominence, but long-term evidence on pain attributable to these screws is limited.
objectives: Determine the rate of postoperative S2AI screw-related pain after adult spinal deformity surgery with a minimum 2-year follow-up.
Assess the rate of reoperation and identify risk factors for postoperative S2AI screw-related pain.
clinical_question: P: Adults undergoing surgery for spinal deformity; I: pelvic fixation with S2AI screws; C: no alternative fixation group specified; O: rates of screw-related pain and reoperation, and factors associated with screw-related pain, after a minimum 2-year follow-up.
study_design: Retrospective cohort based on a review of consecutive patients' records. A single surgeon performed the operations between August 2015 and December 2017.

population.description: Adults with spinal deformity who underwent long fusion with pelvic S2AI screw fixation. Of 160 patients identified as having pelvic fixation, 83 met the study criteria; 53 had complete patient-reported outcome data for the subgroup analysis.
inclusion_criteria: Pelvic fixation using S2AI screws during a long fusion, defined as over 5 levels
A minimum of 2-year clinical and radiographic follow-up

interventions: Long fusion with pelvic S2AI screw fixation
comparators: Patients with versus without postoperative S2AI screw-related pain

primary: Frequency of postoperative S2AI screw-related pain and factors associated with that pain
secondary: Radiographic S2AI screw findings, including loosening, breakage, nonunion and other hardware complications; loosening was defined by radiolucency greater than 1mm around a screw
Intraoperative and postoperative complications, reoperations and S2AI screw removal
Preoperative and 2-year postoperative Scoliosis Research Society-22 (SRS) function, pain and total scores and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) scores in the subgroup with complete questionnaires
Preoperative and 2-year postoperative sagittal vertical axis (SVA) and central sacral vertical line (CSVL) measurements in that subgroup

statistical_methods: Categorical variables were compared with chi-square tests and continuous variables with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Linear regression assessed associations between collected variables and S2AI screw-related pain using SAS software. The subgroup analysis used independent and paired t-tests for preoperative and postoperative scores, operative data and radiographic data. P <0.05 was the threshold for statistical significance.
follow_up: A minimum of 2-year clinical and radiographic follow-up; standing radiographs were assessed at 1-year and 2-year visits, and the subgroup questionnaires and radiographic measurements were assessed preoperatively and at 2-year follow-up.
interpretation: At a minimum 2-year follow-up, the authors report S2AI screw-related pain in 9.6% of patients and screw removal in 3.4%. Screw size and number did not predict pain, and radiographic screw abnormalities corresponded poorly with symptoms. The authors describe an association between L5-S1 interbody fusion and pain, while proposing that greater mechanical stress at the distal construct might contribute; this mechanism remains speculative. Patient-reported outcomes and alignment improved in both groups, although the pain group had smaller changes in ODI, SRS total and SRS pain, alongside larger changes in SVA and SRS function. The authors suggest that screw-related pain may adversely affect patients despite deformity correction.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The observed S2AI screw-related pain rate was lower than the previously reported 20% rate for pain associated with iliac screws. The authors place their 18.1% (15/83) overall reoperation rate within a previously reported range of 8.8-23%. They compare their weak correspondence between imaging abnormalities and pain with reports by Smith et al of predominantly asymptomatic S2AI screw lucencies in 10.4% of cases and by Mazur et al of partial periscrew lucency in 27% of patients without S2AI screw-related complications. Ha et al reported no relationship between the number of fused segments and SI joint degeneration, although 75% of their patients developed degeneration. The authors also relate their multi-rod observations to Banno et al’s report of more iliac screw loosening with multi-rod constructs; they note that differences between the studies might reflect Banno et al’s 1 year follow-up and different pelvic fixation technique.
clinical_implications: Pain attributed to S2AI screws may occur without a corresponding radiographic abnormality; conversely, a radiographic screw finding does not necessarily indicate pain.

The authors suggest that L5-S1 interbody fusion might increase forces transmitted to the SI joints and thereby contribute to pain or instrumentation failure, but present this as a possible explanation.

The authors propose that greater sagittal alignment change might increase stress around the distal construct. They consider the contribution of coronal alignment uncertain given the small differences and relatively high variability.
practice_implications: The authors recommend placing greater emphasis on clinical examination than on radiographic findings when evaluating patients after S2AI screw fixation.
limitations: Assessment of SI joint pain during follow-up relied largely on patients’ subjective reports of lumbosacral pain or prominent instrumentation, without a specific SI joint examination.
The authors did not perform diagnostic injections in patients reporting pain around the SI joint.
Radiographic assessment of S2AI screws was subjective and might have missed subtle periscrew haloing.
Excluding patients with previous iliac screw fixation reduced the number eligible for analysis.
open_questions: The relationship between radiographic SI joint degeneration and clinically significant pain remains insufficiently described.
The authors question whether a larger sample would clarify the influence of the small observed coronal-alignment differences on postoperative S2AI screw-related pain.
future_directions: The authors call for prospective assessment of S2AI screw-related SI joint pain in a larger cohort that includes patients both with and without previous iliac screw fixation.

main_findings.description: S2AI screw-related pain occurred after adult spinal deformity surgery.
main_findings.context: 83 patients met the inclusion criteria; follow-up was at least 2 years.

main_findings.description: Radiographs showed an S2AI screw-related complication.
main_findings.context: Among patients with a radiographic finding, 2 had S2AI screw-related pain (22.2%). The authors reported poor correspondence between these findings and pain.

main_findings.description: S2AI screw removal was reported for the overall cohort, although the stated denominator differs from the cohort of 83 patients.
main_findings.context: The abstract and conclusion also report 3.4% without a denominator.

main_findings.description: S2AI screw size and number did not significantly predict screw-related pain.
main_findings.context: Group-specific sizes, screw counts and p-values are detailed in subgroup_analyses.

main_findings.description: S2AI screw bending was more frequent in patients with screw-related pain than in those without pain.
The pain group underwent reoperation more frequently than the no-pain group.
main_findings.context: Pain group (N = 8) versus no-pain group (N = 75), as reported in Table 3.

main_findings.description: The reported frequency of S2AI screw removal differed between the pain and no-pain groups.
main_findings.context: Table 3 reports these values for the pain group (N = 8) and no-pain group (N = 75). The accompanying prose instead states 25% versus 0% (p < 0.001) and says that 2 (25%) patients with pain elected removal.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: The overall intraoperative complication rate was 27.7%, and the postoperative complication rate was 19.3%. The overall reoperation rate was 18.1% (15/83).
notable_adverse_events: Intraoperative complications: 20 (26.67%) in the no-pain group and 3 (37.5%) in the pain group; p = 0.52.
Dural tear: 17 (22.67%) in the no-pain group and 2 (25%) in the pain group; p = 0.88. The overall rate reported in the prose was 22.9%.
Loss of intraoperative signals: 5 (6.67%) in the no-pain group and 1 (12.5%) in the pain group; p = 0.544. The overall rate of neuromonitoring loss reported in the prose was 7.2%.
Postoperative complications: 15 (20%) in the no-pain group and 1 (12.5%) in the pain group; p = 0.61. No postoperative paralysis was reported.
S2AI screw-related radiographic findings: 7 (9.3%) in the no-pain group and 2 (25%) in the pain group; p = 0.176.
S2AI screw loosening: 5 (6.0%) overall; 5 (6.67%) in the no-pain group and 0 (0%) in the pain group; p = 0.45.
S2AI screw fracture: 3 (3.6%) overall; 2 (2.67%) in the no-pain group and 1 (12.5%) in the pain group; p = 0.16 in Table 3.
S2AI screw bending: 1 (1.2%) overall; 0 (0%) in the no-pain group and 1 (12.5%) in the pain group; p = 0.002.
Wound complication: 4 (5.33%) in the no-pain group and 1 (12.5%) in the pain group; p = 0.42.

Gastrointestinal complication: 3 (4%) in the no-pain group and 0 (0%) in the pain group; p = 0.56. Ileus accounted for 2 (2.67%) versus 0 (0%); p = 0.64. Vomiting accounted for 1 (1.33%) versus 0 (0%); p = 0.74.

Cardiac complication: 6 (8%) in the no-pain group and 0 (0%) in the pain group; p = 0.41. Tachycardic/Hypotensive events occurred in 2 (2.67%) versus 0 (0%); p = 0.64. Edema occurred in 1 (1.33%) versus 0 (0%); p = 0.74. Cardiac/Respiratory Arrest occurred in 1 (1.33%) versus 0 (0%); p = 0.74.

Pulmonary complication: 4 (5.33%) in the no-pain group and 0 (0%) in the pain group; p = 0.42. Respiratory Distress occurred in 2 (2.67%) versus 0 (0%); p = 0.64. Pleural Effusion occurred in 2 (2.67%) versus 0 (0%); p = 0.64.
Neurological complication: 1 (1.33%) in the no-pain group and 0 (0%) in the pain group; p = 0.74.
DVT/PE: 2 (2.67%) in the no-pain group and 0 (0%) in the pain group; p = 0.64.
Anemia: 2 (2.67%) in the no-pain group and 0 (0%) in the pain group; p = 0.64.

subgroup_analyses: Baseline characteristics, no-pain group (N = 75) versus pain group (N = 8): age 56.8 + 12.3 versus 54.6 + 4.7 years (p = 0.34); female sex 57 (76.0) versus 5 (62.5) (p = 0.19); BMI 26.5 + 7.1 versus 24.2 + 3.2 (p = 0.12). The authors reported no baseline demographic differences.

Operative characteristics, no-pain group versus pain group: prior spinal instrumentation 36 (48%) versus 5 (62.5%) (p = 0.44); levels fused 13.3 + 5.0 versus 15.5 + 11.8 (p = 0.25); operative time 500 + 132 versus 613 + 115 min (p = 0.10); EBL 1557 + 945 versus 1825 + 1022 mL (p = 0.47).

Interbody procedures, no-pain group versus pain group: OLIF/TLIF 71 (94.67%) versus 8 (100%) (p = 0.56); TLIF 65 (86.67%) versus 8 (100%) (p = 0.27); OLIF 6 (7.1%) versus 0 (0%) (p = 0.41). By level, L1-L2 was 5 (6.67%) versus 0 (0%) (p = 0.45), L2-L3 was 5 (6.67%) versus 0 (0%) (p = 0.45), L3-L4 was 12 (16%) versus 2 (25%) (p = 0.52), L4-L5 was 19 (25.3%) versus 3 (37.5%) (p = 0.46), and L5-S1 was 55 (73.3%) versus 8 (100%) (p = 0.094). The conclusion describes a strong correlation between L5-S1 anterior column fusion and pain, whereas the tabulated L5-S1 comparison has p = 0.094.

Instrumentation, no-pain group versus pain group: intraoperative screw repositioning 3 (4%) versus 0 (0%) (p = 0.56); supplemental iliac screw placement 12 (16%) versus 2 (25%) (p = 0.52); screw diameter 8.53 + 0.26 versus 8.5 + 0 mm (p = 0.73); screw length 85.1 + 6.46 versus 87.5 + 4.63 mm (p = 0.31).

Number of S2AI screws, no-pain group versus pain group: 2 screws in 69 (92.0%) versus 7 (87.5%) (p = 0.57); 3 screws in 2 (2.67%) versus 0 (0%) (p = 0.64); and 4 screws in 4 (5.33%) versus 1 (12.5%) (p = 0.42). The authors reported no operative-variable differences between groups.
Among the 8 patients with pain, 5 (62.5%) underwent revision index surgery, 8 (100%) had TLIF at L5-S1, and 2 (25%) had S2AI screw-related radiographic findings: fracture in 1 and bending in 1.

The patient-reported outcome sub-analysis included 53 patients: 46 without pain and 7 with pain. For osteotomy, PCO was reported in 32 (80) versus 6 (85.7), PSO in 5 (12.5) versus 0 (0), and VCR in 3 (7.5) versus 1 (14.3), respectively; the osteotomy comparison had p = 0.18. Rod counts of 2, 3, 4 and 5 were 2 (4.4), 28 (60.9), 15 (32.6) and 1 (2.2) without pain, versus 0 (0), 7 (100), 0 (0) and 0 (0) with pain.

SVA in the no-pain sub-analysis group: preoperative 5.3 + 5.7 cm, postoperative 3.2 + 2.5 cm, mean difference 2.1 + 4.8 cm, and paired p = 0.005 in Table 5. The results prose instead gives p < 0.0001 for the preoperative-to-postoperative comparison. In the pain group: preoperative 8.2 + 5.2 cm, postoperative 4.2 + 4.4 cm, mean difference 4.0 + 4.9 cm, and paired p = 0.12. Between-group p-values were 0.21 preoperatively and 0.34 postoperatively.

CSVL in the no-pain sub-analysis group: preoperative 3.1 + 2.9 cm, postoperative 1.6 + 1.5 cm, mean difference 1.5 + 2.3 cm, and paired p <0.0001. In the pain group: preoperative 2.6 + 1.7 cm, postoperative 1.5 + 1.2 cm, mean difference 1.1 + 1.0 cm, and paired p = 0.033 in Table 5; the results prose gives p = 0.03. Between-group p-values were 0.61 preoperatively and 0.85 postoperatively.

ODI in the no-pain sub-analysis group: preoperative 38.6 + 18.5, postoperative 18.7 + 16.8, mean difference 19.9 + 16.9, and paired p <0.0001 in Table 5; the results prose gives p < 0.001. In the pain group: preoperative 44.6 + 13.7, postoperative 26.0 + 11.0, mean difference 18.6 + 23.8, and paired p = 0.084 in Table 5; the results prose gives p = 0.08. Between-group p-values were 0.42 preoperatively and 0.29 postoperatively.

SRS total in the no-pain sub-analysis group: preoperative 63.1 + 58.7, postoperative 88.0 + 16.0, mean difference 24.9 + 15.4, and paired p <0.0001 in Table 5. In the pain group: preoperative 58.7 + 13.8, postoperative 80.3 + 14.6, mean difference 21.6 + 19.2, and paired p = 0.025 in Table 5; the results prose gives p = 0.03. Between-group p-values were 0.48 preoperatively and 0.24 postoperatively.

SRS pain in the no-pain sub-analysis group: preoperative 2.8 + 0.9, postoperative 3.9 + 1.0, mean difference 1.4 + 1.1, and paired p <0.0001. In the pain group: preoperative 2.4 + 0.4, postoperative 3.4 + 0.9, mean difference 1.0 + 1.1, and paired p = 0.51; this change was not statistically significant. Between-group p-values were 0.32 preoperatively and 0.20 postoperatively.

SRS function in the no-pain sub-analysis group: preoperative 2.9 + 0.9, postoperative 3.9 + 0.8, mean difference 0.9 + 0.8, and paired p <0.0001. In the pain group: preoperative 2.8 + 0.6, postoperative 4.1 + 0.8, mean difference 1.2 + 0.5, and paired p = 0.0007. Between-group p-values were 0.75 preoperatively and 0.57 postoperatively. The mean change was larger in the pain group.
secondary_results: The 83 included patients comprised 62 (74.7%) women and 21 (25.3%) men; mean BMI was 26.3 (+6.9), and mean age was 56.6 (+11.7) years.

There were 41 (49.4%) primary surgeries and 42 (50.6%) revision surgeries. Mean fusion length was 13.5 (+5.0) levels, and the mean number of S2AI screws was 2.13 (+0.5). Two screws were used in 76 (91.6%) patients, 3 in 2 (2.4%), and 4 in 5 (6.0%). The most frequent screw size was 8.5 90mm, used in 47 patients (56.6%).
An OLIF or TLIF was performed in 79 (95.2%) patients. The prose reports TLIF in 73 patients (85.9%) and OLIF in 6 patients (7.2%); L5-S1 was the most frequent level, in 63 patients (75.9%).
The prose reports intraoperative S2AI screw repositioning in 3 (3.8%) patients and supplemental iliac screws in 14 (17.5%) patients.

Pseudarthrosis was described as the most frequent reason for reoperation (6%). Table 3 reports reoperation for Pseudoarthrosis in 4 (5.33%) patients without pain and 1 (12.5%) with pain (p = 0.42); PJK in 2 (2.67%) versus 0 (0%) (p = 0.64); Implant Failure in 2 (2.67%) versus 1 (12.5%) (p = 0.15); Wound Complication in 4 (5.33%) versus 1 (12.5%) (p = 0.42); Radiculopathy in 1 (1.33%) versus 0 (0%) (p = 0.74); UE/LE Weakness in 1 (1.33%) versus 0 (0%) (p = 0.74); and Flat Back Syndrome in 2 (2.67%) versus 0 (0%) (p = 0.64).

For patients with pain, the prose reports subsequent revision surgery in 3 (37.5%) of 8, while Table 3 reports reoperation in 4 (50%). It reports that 2 (25%) elected S2AI screw removal, while Table 3 reports removal in 3 (37.5%). The discussion states that 3 removal and revision procedures occurred at 20, 24 and 43 months and that pain improved afterward.

Within the pain group, the patient table describes bilateral S2AI screw removal for pain in Patient 3 at 43 months and Patient 6 at 20 months. Patient 7, who had an S2AI screw fracture, underwent revision fusion from T10-Pelvis at 24 Months for Pseudoarthrosis. Patient 8 had S2AI screw bending without revision surgery.

tables.summary: In the complete-outcomes subgroup, both groups generally improved in patient-reported scores and alignment, although within-group statistical significance varied. The pain group had larger mean changes in SVA and SRS function. The table's paired SVA P-value for the no-pain group is 0.005, while the results prose reports p < 0.0001; the table's paired SRS total P-value for the pain group is 0.025, while the prose reports p = 0.03. The table identifies independent t-tests for between-group P-values and paired t-tests for within-group P-values.

main_conclusion: After a minimum 2-year follow-up of S2AI fixation for adult spinal deformity, the authors report screw-related pain in 9.6% of patients and screw removal in 3.4%. They describe a strong relationship between L5-S1 anterior column fusion and pain, but not between pain and screw size or number; radiographic screw findings corresponded poorly with symptoms. Alignment and patient-reported measures improved after surgery, with larger SVA and SRS function changes in the pain group.
narrative_summary: This retrospective cohort examined S2AI pelvic fixation after long fusion for adult spinal deformity. It included 83 patients with at least 2-year clinical and radiographic follow-up; 53 also had complete preoperative and postoperative outcome data for subgroup analysis. S2AI screw-related pain occurred in 8 (9.6%) patients. Radiographic screw findings occurred in 10.8%, but only 22.2% of patients with those findings reported screw-related pain. Screw size and number did not predict pain. All 8 patients with pain had L5-S1 interbody fusion; the authors describe a relationship with pain, although the operative table reports P-value 0.094 for the L5-S1 comparison. Reoperation was more frequent in the pain group, at 50% versus 14.67% (p = 0.01). The article reports an overall screw-removal rate of 3.4%, but its removal counts and denominators differ across the prose and tables. Patient-reported outcomes and alignment generally improved after surgery; the pain group showed larger changes in SVA and SRS function. The authors favor clinical assessment over reliance on radiographic screw findings when evaluating postoperative pain. Interpretation is limited by the retrospective design, subjective assessment of SI joint pain, potentially missed subtle radiographic loosening, and exclusion of patients with prior iliac screw fixation.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Study design: retrospective cohort. The objective was to measure S2AI screw-related pain and identify its risk factors after adult spinal deformity surgery, with at least 2 years of follow-up. The study included 83 consecutive patients treated between August 2015 and December 2017. The authors examined screw complications and pain, used linear regression to assess potential risk factors, and analyzed operative, radiographic, SRS, and ODI data in a subgroup of 53 patients. S2AI screw-related pain occurred in 9.6% of patients. Radiographic screw complications occurred in 10.8%; among patients with those findings, 22.2% had screw-related pain. S2A1 screws were removed in 3.4% of all patients. SRS, ODI, sagittal vertical axis (SVA), and coronal alignment improved after surgery. The pain group had larger preoperative-to-postoperative mean differences than the no-pain group in SRS function (1.2 + 0.5 vs 0.9 + 0.8) and SVA (4.0 + 4.9cm vs 2.1 + 4.8cm). Screw size and number did not predict pain, and radiographic findings did not correlate with clinical outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Correcting adult spinal deformity while avoiding complications is difficult. Pseudarthrosis at the distal end of a long fusion frequently necessitates another operation. At the lumbosacral junction, forces from the proximally fused segments contribute to this problem; pelvic fixation supplies additional distal support. Iliac screws and bolts can protect S1 pedicle screws and improve fusion, but connecting their lateral fixation points to proximal instrumentation may require a connector that introduces another possible point of failure. Iliac screws can also be prominent near the posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS); clinically important prominence has been reported in up to 20%. S2-alar-iliac (S2AI) fixation starts deeper and more medially than conventional iliac screw fixation and is intended to avoid prominent hardware. Although prior research compared the techniques, long-term evidence about pain attributable to S2AI screws remained limited. The authors sought to establish whether postoperative screw pain and reoperation rates were low and to explore factors associated with S2AI screw-related pain.

document_sections.heading: Methods Patient Population
document_sections.content: The hospital Institutional Review Board approved the study (IRB-AAAS0556). The authors retrospectively reviewed adult spinal deformity operations performed by one surgeon (LGL), defining a long fusion as over 5 levels. They identified 160 patients who underwent pelvic fixation from August 2015 to December 2017 using CPT code 22848. Eligibility required age over 18 years old, pelvic S2AI screw fixation, and at least 2 years of clinical and radiographic follow-up. Patients under 18 years old, those with previous iliac screw fixation, those without S2AI pelvic screws, and those with inadequate follow-up were excluded. The final analysis comprised 83 patients.

document_sections.heading: Data Collection
document_sections.content: Recorded characteristics were age, sex, BMI, osteoporosis history, and psychiatric history. Operative records supplied the number of fused levels, screw dimensions and count, intraoperative complications, and intraoperative screw exchange. Standing full-body radiographs from the 1-year and 2-year follow-up visits were assessed by one senior orthopedic resident (ASH) for loosening, breakage, nonunion, and other hardware problems. Radiographic loosening meant a radiolucent area greater than 1mm around a screw, termed a halo sign. Clinical notes were examined for postoperative S2AI screw-related pain. SI joint pain was identified from patients’ subjective reports elicited by the senior author during follow-up, without SI joint-specific examinations.

document_sections.heading: Patient-Reported Outcomes Data
document_sections.content: The subgroup assessment used Scoliosis Research Society-22 (SRS) and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) questionnaires. The SRS-22 measures of interest were function, pain, and total scores. Only patients with both preoperative and 2year postoperative SRS-22 and ODI questionnaires entered this analysis. For patients with complete questionnaires, operative information included rod count and posterior column osteotomy (PCO), pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO), or vertebral column resection (VCR). Preoperative and 2-year postoperative radiographs were used to measure sagittal vertical axis (SVA) and central sacral vertical line (CSVL). The patient-demographics table presents age, female sex, and BMI separately for patients with and without pain.

document_sections.heading: Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: Demographic and operative characteristics were compared according to S2AI screw-related pain at 2year follow-up. Categorical variables were tested with chi-square tests and continuous variables with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. The authors used linear regression in SAS software to examine associations between the collected variables and S2AI pain. In patients with complete patient-reported outcomes, independent and paired t-tests assessed preoperative and postoperative SRS/ODI scores alongside operative and radiographic data. Statistical significance was set at P <0.05.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: Among 83 eligible patients, 8 (9.6%) reported S2AI screw-related pain. The cohort included 62 (74.7%) women and 21 (25.3%) men; mean BMI was 26.3 (+6.9), and mean age was 56.6 (+11.7) years. Baseline demographics did not differ between pain groups. There were 41 (49.4%) primary operations and 42 (50.6%) revision operations. Fusion covered an average of 13.5 (+5.0) levels, and an average of 2.13 (+0.5) S2AI screws were implanted. Screw counts were 2 in 76 (91.6%) patients, 3 in 2 (2.4%), and 4 in 5 (6.0%); the most frequent size was 8.5 90mm in 47 patients (56.6%). OLIF or TLIF was performed in 79 (95.2%) patients: TLIF in 73 patients (85.9%) and OLIF in 6 patients (7.2%). L5-S1 was the most frequent level, in 63 patients (75.9%). Intraoperative S2AI screw repositioning occurred in 3 (3.8%) patients, while 14 (17.5%) received at least one additional iliac screw. Operative variables did not differ between pain groups; the operative-information table provides group comparisons. Overall intraoperative complication, postoperative complication, and reoperation rates were 27.7%, 19.3%, and 18.1%, respectively. Dural tear (22.9%) and loss of intraoperative neuromonitoring (7.2%) were the leading intraoperative complications. No postoperative paralysis occurred, and intraoperative complication rates did not differ by pain status. Radiographic S2AI screw-related findings were the most common postoperative complication, occurring in 10.8%: loosening in 5 (6.0%) patients, breakage in 3 (3.6%), and bending in 1 (1.2%). Bending was more frequent in the pain group than the no-pain group (12.5% vs 0%; p = 0.002). Pseudarthrosis was the leading reason for reoperation overall (6%). Among patients with screw-related pain, the narrative identifies S2AI screw removal as the most common reoperation (25%); among those without pain, pseudarthrosis and wound complications were the most common reasons (5.33% each). Reoperation was more frequent with pain than without it (50% vs 14.67%; p = 0.01). The narrative also reports a higher screw-removal rate with pain (25% vs 0%; p < 0.001), while its complications-and-reoperations table lists 3 (37.5%) versus 0 (0%) for removal. That table additionally details complications and reoperation indications by group. Of the 8 patients with pain, 5 (62.5%) had revision index operations and 8 (100%) had TLIFs at L5-S1. Radiographic screw findings affected 2 (25%) of these 8 patients: 1 S2A1 screw fracture and 1 S2A1 screw bend. Subsequent revision surgery was reported for 3 (37.5%), and 2 (25%) elected screw removal. The narrative gives an overall removal rate of 3.4% (3/87 patients), although the analyzed cohort is described as 83 patients. The table of painful-screw cases describes each patient’s age, diagnosis, index procedure, imaging findings, and subsequent surgery. In the subgroup of 53 patient, the no-pain group improved after treatment in SRS total (63.1 + 58.7 vs 88.0 + 16.0; p < 0.0001), SRS pain (2.8 + 0.9 vs 3.9 + 1.0; p < 0.0001), SRS function (2.9 + 0.9 vs 3.9 + 0.8; p < 0.0001), and ODI (38.6 + 18.5 vs 18.7 + 16.8; p < 0.001). The pain group also improved in SRS total (58.7 + 13.8 vs 80.3 + 14.6; p = 0.03), SRS pain (2.4 + 0.4 vs 3.4 + 0.9; p = 0.51), SRS function (2.8 + 0.6 vs 4.1 + 0.8; p = 0.0007), and ODI (44.6 + 13.7 vs 26.0 + 11.0; p = 0.08), with varying statistical significance. In the no-pain group, SVA fell from 5.3 + 5.7 to 3.2 + 2.5 (p < 0.0001) and CSVL from 3.1 + 2.9 to 1.6 + 1.5 (p < 0.0001). Corresponding pain-group changes were SVA, 8.2 + 5.2 vs 4.2 + 4.4 (p = 0.12), and CSVL, 2.6 + 1.7 vs 1.5 + 1.2 (p = 0.03). Three-rod fixation was used in 60.9% of the no-pain group and 100% of the pain group. Operative treatment was similar between groups: PCO was performed in 85.7% with pain versus 80% without pain, and VCR in 14.3% versus 7.5% (p = 0.18). The outcomes-and-measurements table also presents preoperative and postoperative values, changes, osteotomy types, and rod counts by group.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors describe S2AI fixation as a technique that could lessen pelvic-fixation pain while preserving fusion and reducing reoperation in adult spinal deformity surgery. Its medial, deep entry point aligns more directly with the S1 screw and facilitates rod placement. Potential concerns remain hardware prominence and SI joint pain because the screw passes from the sacrum across the SI joint into the ilium. In this cohort, 9.6% reported screw-related pain after at least 2 years, without radiographic findings reliably corresponding to pain. This rate was below a previously reported iliac-screw pain rate of 20%. The authors attribute reduced prominence to the S2AI starting point, without sacrificing screw length or thickness. The no-pain group had higher mean BMI than the pain group (26.5 + 7.1 vs 24.2 + 3.2), which the authors consider another factor mitigating prominence. They state that women were more likely to report pain, without statistical significance; the demographic table lists 57 (76.0) women without pain and 5 (62.5) with pain. Most implanted screws were 8.5 90mm, described as sturdier than many pelvic screws in prior literature. Neither screw size nor screw count had a statistically significant association with pain. Additional iliac screws were present in 25% of the pain group; the authors interpret this as further suggesting that iliac screws can generate pain. They report an association between L5-S1 anterior-column interbody fusion and S2AI screw-related pain: all 8 patients with pain had L5-S1 interbody fusion, compared with 73.3% without pain. They propose, rather than establish, that rigid distal fixation could transmit greater cantilevering forces to the SI joints, potentially increasing joint motion, pain, arthritis, or hardware failure. Fused-level counts did not differ significantly between the no-pain (13.3 + 5.0) and pain (15.5 + 11.8) groups; the authors did not expect the approximately one-level difference they describe to substantially raise SI joint forces. In a cited study, Ha et al found no relationship between fused-segment count and SI joint degeneration after fusion to the sacrum, although 75% of their patients developed SI joint degeneration. The authors note limited evidence linking radiographic degeneration to clinically meaningful pain. Reoperation differed significantly by pain status. The discussion reports overall S2AI screw removal as 3.4% (3/87 patients), revision surgery in 50% of the pain group, and screw removal in 37.5% of that group. It states that the 3 screw-removal and revision cases occurred 20, 24 and 43 months after surgery and that pain improved afterward; these accounts do not fully align with the earlier narrative and individual cases in the patient table. Revision surgery occurred in 14.7% of the no-pain group, with none revised for an S2AI screw. Only 2 of 8 patients with pain had radiographic findings, namely fracture or bending; the authors state that only 1 of these 2 underwent revision for a fractured screw. Total reoperation was 18.1% (15/83), compared with previously reported revision rates of 8.8-23%. Among 9 patients with radiographic findings, only 2 had pain (22.2%); fracture and bending were the radiographic findings associated with pain. Smith et al reported predominantly asymptomatic S2AI screw lucencies in 10.4% of cases. Mazur et al reported partial periscrew lucency in 27% of patients, none of whom had S2AI screw-related complications. The authors therefore favor clinical examination over imaging findings when evaluating patients after S2AI fixation. Patient-reported outcomes improved in both groups, although statistical significance varied. Smaller mean changes in ODI, SRS total, and SRS pain among patients with pain are interpreted as suggesting an adverse effect from screw-related pain despite deformity correction. The greater SRS function change in the pain group might reflect greater activity and consequent SI joint movement. All patients with pain had 3 rods. Banno et al reported more iliac screw loosening with multi-rod constructs and proposed concentrated stress at distal junctional segments, but found no significant effect of loosening on postoperative spinopelvic measurements or ODI. The authors suggest that differences from Banno et al might relate to that study’s 1 year of follow-up and different pelvic fixation. Both preoperative SVA and its mean change were higher in the pain group; the authors consider greater sagittal correction a likely source of increased distal-construct stress. Postoperative coronal alignment did not appear to influence pain in this subgroup (1.5 + 1.2cm vs 1.6 + 1.5cm; p = 0.85), although differences of less than 1cm for most coronal measures and relatively high variability could require greater statistical power. The figure captions describe radiographs of Patient 1 at 6 days after the index procedure and at 20 months, including an image one day after S2AI screw removal; they also describe Patient 8 radiographs at 8 days and 26 months, the latter showing a bent screw. No SI joint-specific physical examination was performed. The authors describe reproducing pain by manual palpation or compression around the SI joints and note that SI joint-specific examinations have historically had low sensitivity and specificity. They mention CT-guided injection as another possible diagnostic and therapeutic approach, but did not perform diagnostic injections because only 8/83 patients described SI-region pain and 3/8 required screw removal. They also report not using diagnostic imaging to establish screw-related pain in this selected group after history and palpation reproduced it. Study limitations include the retrospective cohort, difficulty assessing SI joint pain when follow-up relied largely on subjective lumbosacral pain or perceived hardware prominence, absence of SI joint-specific examinations, subjective radiographic assessment that could miss subtle halos, and exclusion of patients with prior iliac screw fixation, which reduced eligibility. The authors call for prospective evaluation in a larger cohort, including patients with and without prior iliac screw fixation, to assess S2AI screw-related SI joint pain.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: After at least 2 years of follow-up following S2AI fixation for adult spinal deformity, screw-related pain occurred in 9.6% of patients and screw removal in 3.4%. The authors report a strong correlation between L5-S1 anterior-column fusion and pain. Screw dimensions and count did not predict postoperative pain, while radiographic findings had little correspondence with clinical outcomes. CSVL, SVA, ODI, SRS total, SRS pain, and SRS function improved postoperatively across patients; those with pain had larger changes in SVA and SRS function.
